He Bought a Chevrolet Corvette, Drove 686 Miles and Listed It for Sale
23 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
Cars start losing value the moment they are driven off the showroom floor. This is something that surprises owners every time. It was the case for this Chevy Corvette Stingray owner as well. He bought the car in April, drove 700 miles, listed it for sale, but the ‘Vette failed to reach the reserve, so he is now stuck with it.
The car in question is a 2026 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray Coupe 2LT, finished in Blade Silver Metallic over a Sky Cool Gray leather interior, sheltered by a removable roof panel, and riding on alloy wheels measuring 19 inches up front and 20 inches out back.
The driver and passenger sit in heated and ventilated seats with yellow seat belts. The driver gets the relevant driving data via the head-up display and can record track performance with the help of the performance data and video recorder. A Bose sound system provides the soundtrack when the driver has had enough of the V8 orchestra.
Speaking of which, the 6.2-liter LT2 V8 with naturally aspirated firepower pumps out 495 horsepower (502 metric horsepower) when the Z51 package is involved, which is not the case for this car, so it sticks to 490 horsepower (497 metric horsepower) and 470 pound-feet (637 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Cars and Bids Those are enough to make the car rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 2.9 seconds, run the quarter mile in 11.2 seconds, and top out at 194 mph (312 kph). A dual-clutch eight-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure Corvette fashion.
However, the owner did not enjoy much of those. He bought the Chevrolet Corvette Stingray back in April, drove just 686 miles (1,104 kilometers), and listed it for sale. It’s usually either incompatibility, having another car on the way, or the Mrs. telling the Mr. to get rid of it ASAP.
However, the market decides how soon because the first attempt at selling it gloriously failed. The original owner paid $83,965 to go home with it six months ago and listed it for sale for an undisclosed reserve. Bidding stopped at $61,000, and the owner is stuck with the car for the moment.
Not even the clean Carfax report with no mileage discrepancies and no accidents convinced bidders to offer more. Better luck next time. But as time passes, the only way for the value of a car is down, unless it is a rare collectable model, which is not the case.
Besides, this 2026 Chevy Corvette Stingray is lacking three important features: the very sought-after Z51 package, the front lift, and the Magnetic Ride Control. With the seller failing to answer the questions of those interested in the car, no wonder he still has it in his garage.
